input: It is important to note that amine absorption technology has recently been evaluated at pilot scale on gas originating from a cement kiln, and the findings of this evaluation provide valuable insights into how the process performs under real-world operating conditions. Over a period of 90 days, during which the unit handled 12 t of carbon dioxide per day, the system successfully captured 92% of the carbon dioxide present in the treated gas, underscoring the effectiveness of the approach in this setting. In terms of energy requirements, the steam demand was found to be 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, a figure that reflects the considerable energy needed to regenerate the solvent on an ongoing basis so that it can be returned to the absorber for further use. Furthermore, the solvent loss was measured at 1.6 kg per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, highlighting the importance of careful solvent management in maintaining efficient, sustainable, and cost-effective operation over time. It should also be noted that questions remain regarding the longer-term behaviour of the solvent in this environment. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, and further investigation will ultimately be needed in order to fully understand how dust carried over from the kiln might impact solvent condition and, in turn, overall performance during extended periods of operation. Overall, the results demonstrate the significant potential of the process, while also pointing towards areas where additional research could further strengthen confidence going forward.
target:
An amine absorption unit treated gas from a cement kiln at pilot scale. Over 90 days at 12 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. Solvent loss was 1.6 kg per tonne of carbon dioxide captured.

The capture figure is a fraction of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Gas that did not pass through the unit is outside the stated result, and the figure says nothing about kiln output as a whole. Steam demand is the heat supplied to release the captured carbon dioxide from the solvent and return the solvent to the absorber. A demand stated per tonne captured ties the energy cost to output rather than to operating time, and units of different size can be compared on that basis. Solvent loss is stated on the same basis. Solvent leaves a working unit with the treated gas and the captured stream, and by degradation in service; the loss figure is the make-up needed to hold the solvent inventory during the test. Neither figure is a design value. Both were measured on kiln gas at pilot scale, under the gas composition and dust load of the test period.

Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Dust reaches the solvent with the gas, and a longer run could change solvent condition in ways a test of this length does not show. The capture, steam, and solvent figures are stated for the tested period, and no figure is given for extended operation.
